name: Outline
tagline: A team wiki and knowledge base with fast search, nested documents and a clean markdown editor.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: Outline is a nicely built wiki, and for one person the hard parts mostly evaporate. What you actually use solo is nested markdown documents, instant full text search, and a UI that does not fight you, all of which an agent can assemble in an evening on SQLite with FTS5. The cloud product's real work is multiplayer editing, permissions, SSO, and integrations, none of which matter in a single-user notes folder. Worth noting the source is available and self-hostable, so the honest ceiling on DIY is high: you can run the real thing with docker if you want fidelity instead of a toy. Pay for the hosted version when other humans need to read and edit the same page at the same time.
coreLoopDIY: A local single-user wiki: nested markdown documents in SQLite with full text search, backlinks, and an editor that autosaves.
whatYouLose: Slack, Notion, Figma and Google Drive integrations plus the import pipelines
Sharing docs publicly or with granular team permissions
Mobile apps, offline sync, and a search UI that has been tuned for years
SSO, audit logs, and someone else's backups
moatNotes: The moat is other people being in the document. Alone in a wiki, there is no moat, just a text editor with good search.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because a wiki is only worth writing in if colleagues actually read it, and that requires accounts, permissions, notifications, search everyone trusts, and an editor that does not lose a paragraph when two people type at once. Outline also sits where work happens: Slack unfurls, imports from whatever the team used before, single sign-on so nobody has to be onboarded twice. A personal build covers the writing and the finding, which is genuinely most of the daily value for one person, but it covers none of the reasons a company standardizes on a knowledge base.
notes: The unusual case where the paid product is also the open source product, so DIY is a choice about fidelity, not capability.
prompt:
Build a single-user local wiki called "Notebook". Stack, no substitutions: Next.js 15 with the App Router, TypeScript, Tailwind, better-sqlite3. No auth, no accounts, no cloud services, no telemetry, no analytics.

Data model in SQLite (file at ./data/notebook.db, created on first run):
- documents: id, parent_id nullable, title, body markdown, emoji nullable, archived boolean, created_at, updated_at
- an FTS5 virtual table over title and body, kept in sync with triggers
- links: from_doc_id, to_doc_id, derived on save from [[Wiki Style]] references in the body

UI:
- Two pane layout. Left: collapsible document tree built from parent_id, drag to reparent, plus a "New document" button and an archive toggle. Right: the document.
- Editor is a plain textarea with markdown, rendered preview toggled by a button. Autosave 600ms after typing stops, show a small "saved" indicator. No rich text editor library, no ProseMirror.
- Cmd+K opens a search palette that queries FTS5 and shows title plus a highlighted snippet, arrow keys to move, Enter to open.
- Document footer lists backlinks resolved from the links table.
- Support [[Title]] links: on click, open the matching document or create it as a child of the current one.

Extras that are in scope:
- Export all documents as a zip of markdown files mirroring the tree structure.
- Import a folder of markdown files from a path given in a form field.
- Trash: archived documents are hidden from the tree but restorable.

Explicitly out of scope, do not build: multiplayer editing, comments, sharing links, permissions, users, Slack or Google integrations, mobile app, offline sync.

Provide a README with setup steps, npm scripts for dev and build, and a .env.example holding only PORT. Seed the database with three example nested documents so the tree is not empty on first load.
